provenance.agent: Claude Code · Opus 5.5 · audit burn-down session 3

props.title: Is lev worth it?
props.subtitle: 4 outside seats (GPT-6, GLM 5.3, clean Opus, clean Fable) on a neutral fact sheet: 4 of 4 say radically simplify. Plus 16 choices.

props.label: OUTSIDE PANEL
props.title: Same brief, four model families, no repo access

props.content:
| Seat | Verdict | In its words |
|---|---|---|
| codex | Radically simplify | "Lev has earned an extraction trial, not another expansion cycle." |
| glm | Radically simplify: the alternative, with two changes | "Jarvis is real working software; the framework around it is consuming the project." |
| opus-clean | Radically simplify, anchored on Jarvis rather than a new framework | "Why not the alternative as written: a "CLI builder + MCP builder" is framework v2 waiting to happen." |
| fable-clean | Radically simplify | "If an agent needs 5,661 words to avoid breaking things, the tests are wrong, not the agent." |

- **Fact sheet:** `~/.local/state/lev/tribunal/n1-followups-20260927/prompt-worth-it.md` (your question quoted word for word).
- **Caveat:** the brief was measured by an agent inside the repo; the commit sample is hand-classified.

props.label: MY ANSWER
props.title: Claude, this session (informed, so weigh it less)

props.content:
**Yes, but not in this shape.** Tonight's numbers, all re-checked by me:
- 60 of 98 sampled commits are governance, 9 are user-facing. 12 of 50 gates are enforced and none run automatically.
- `lev status` exits 2, `lev task list` fails, `lev search` goes to an unimplemented catalog.
- Jarvis imports lev in 117 files; the next app, 17. 20,756 tracked files sit in Python virtualenvs.

**What is worth keeping** are the ideas that nothing else has together: only one module decides truth, every effect leaves a receipt, gates only ratchet forward, and one declaration projects to CLI, MCP and HTTP.

**What is not worth it** is the breadth: 44 core packages, 65 plugins and 42 crates for one operator and one real consumer. Breadth creates split-brain; split-brain creates rulings, records and vocabulary; those become more for every agent to read. This session is the example: hours of work, zero user-facing change.

**Your alternative is closer than it sounds.** Poly already is the CLI/MCP/HTTP builder, built from module declarations. "Gates + builders" = poly + the 12 enforced gates + the modules Jarvis actually reaches. That is a cut, not a rewrite.

**What I would do:** freeze new modules, records and rulings for 30 days; delete the virtualenvs; make each declared gate run or delete it; archive what Jarvis does not reach; rerun the 14/15 DNA experiment blind against a one-page contract; track user-facing commit share weekly. Caveat: I spent this session inside the repo's own canon, so weigh the four outside seats above mine.

props.label: BLIND CLI GUESSES
props.title: "If you were going to do this, what would you type?"

props.content:
Blind first commands per seat. Families: codex = OpenAI (gpt-6-astra), glm = Z.ai (glm-5.3 via OpenRouter), opus-clean and fable-clean = Anthropic. Sources: seat-blind-cli-codex.md:5-25, seat-blind-cli-glm.md:3-23, and the courier text for the two clean seats.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ready tasks | `lev task list --ready` | `lev task list --status ready` | `lev task list --ready` | `lev task list --ready` | 4/4 `lev task list`; 3/4 `--ready` | Fits the grammar. Not live: `lev task` has only `validate` (verified: `timeout 60 lev task --help`) |
| 2 | Show T1 | `lev task show T1` | same | same | same | 4/4 | Fits. Not live for task |
| 3 | Create under W1 | `lev task create "rate limiter" --workstream W1` | `lev task create --workstream W1 --title "Fix X"` | `lev task create "title" --workstream W1` | `lev task create "rate limiter" --workstream W1` | 4/4 `task create … --workstream W1` | Fits. Not live |
| 4 | Start | `lev task start T1` | same | same | same | 4/4 | Fits. Collides with the reserved `lev work start <agent>` (verified: dna/vernacular.yaml:1004-1027) |
| 5 | Done | `lev task done T1` | same | same | same | 4/4 | Fits. No seat said `close`, which is a locked workflow stage that applies to entities too (verified: dna/vernacular.yaml:720-724) |

| 8 | Delete, then undo | `task delete` then `lev task restore T1` | `task delete` then `lev undo` | `task delete` then `lev undo` | `task delete` then `lev task restore T1` | delete 4/4; undo split 2/2 | The ruling is soft delete plus restore (verified: decision yaml:94). All 4 seats name `restore` as first try or fallback. A root `lev undo` is not in the ruled meta list (:89) |
| 9 | Archive W1 | `lev workstream archive W1` | same | same | same | 4/4 | Fits the grammar, but workstreams have no archived state: active, paused, completed, superseded (verified: core/workstream/src/schema.ts:26). Live path: `lev workstream update W1 --status completed` |
| 10 | Overall state | `lev status` | same | same | same | 4/4 | Matches the ruled meta list (:89) |

| 13 | Web research | `lev research "…" --save` | same | same | same | 4/4 | Allowed only if `research` is a module's own name (owner-verb ruling :88). Inference |
| 14 | Stored context | `lev context search "auth tokens"` | same | `lev context "auth tokens"` | `lev context search "auth tokens"` | 3/4 `context search` | Fits. The opus form uses the bare noun's default verb, which the grammar ruling allows |

The `claim` form matches the ruling "claim = proof" (:95) literally |
| 18 | Timed exclusive lock | `lev task lock T1 --ttl 15m` | `lev task lock T1 --ttl 30m` | same | same | 4/4 `task lock`; 3/4 fall back to `lev task claim` | No seat guessed the reserved `lev work assign`. 3 fallbacks use `claim` to mean a lock, against the ruling |

What the table says: every first try is either `lev <noun> <verb>` or a bare root verb, so the grammar ruling is confirmed by 4 seats from 3 families. For state change (goals 4-7), all 4 seats guessed a named transition first, and 3 of 4 fell back to `lev task update T1 --status …`. Where live lev differs from these guesses: flows (`exec --flow`, not `flow run`), workstream archive (no archived state), and the root verbs outside the ruled list (search, research, init, upgrade, undo).

- **Deleted:** core/a2a, core/agent-fs, core/credential-vault, core/flowmind-memory (0 consumers). core/security is held for the card below.
- **Converged:** Agent Card version + url into core/poly-compiler; mount types + quotas into spec-agentfs; per-agent allowlist into plugins/vault; write rules into core/memory.
- **Checked by me (named test files + typecheck only):** poly-compiler 10/10, vault-engine 27/27, write-gates 15/15, all typechecks exit 0; 0 live references to the deleted packages; `has_spec` now lists only core/security.
- **Operation ids:** `lev workstream list` now reports `workstream.list` (was `workstream.workstream`).
- **Specs:** 20 specs stripped of current-state content; 233 removed items kept as follow-ups under the workstream's `state/follow-ups/`.
- **.lev/tmp:** untracked; the gap report moved to .lev/pm/reports.
- **Not done:** .lev/matrix delete (blocked by the permission classifier); the last reviewer on the operation-id fix was stopped when you said stop running tests.

items.title: Is lev worth it? What happens next
items.insight: **4 of 4 outside seats: radically simplify.** None said continue as-is; none said stop. My own answer is in the section above the cards.
items.detail:
- **codex** (codex exec (model: gpt-6-astra)): Radically simplify. Stop expanding Lev as a general framework and give a small extraction 30 days to prove it deserves to continue (seat-worth-it-codex.md:1). — "Lev has earned an extraction trial, not another expansion cycle."
- **glm** (openrouter z-ai/glm-5.3. The direct Z.ai call returned HTTP 429 (insufficient balance), and the courier fell back to OpenRouter. Exit 0): Radically simplify: the alternative, with two changes. Keep Jarvis and the runtime it actually imports, and keep the 12 enforced gates as CI (seat-worth-it-glm.md:7). — "Jarvis is real working software; the framework around it is consuming the project."
- **opus-clean** (opus (clean Plan agent)): Radically simplify, anchored on Jarvis rather than a new framework. — "Why not the alternative as written: a "CLI builder + MCP builder" is framework v2 waiting to happen."
- **fable-clean** (fable (clean Plan agent)): Radically simplify. Not the alternative as written, but a version that keeps the one thing that might be real. — "If an agent needs 5,661 words to avoid breaking things, the tests are wrong, not the agent."
- **They agree:** Jarvis is the one real consumer; freeze framework and governance growth now; delete the tracked virtualenvs; archive, don't destroy; end 30 days with a measured go/no-go.
- **They split on:** whether a CLI + MCP builder is just "framework v2" (Opus, codex) or the core of the plan (Fable, GLM); how fast to cut; whether to rerun the 14/15 DNA experiment first (Opus, Fable).

options.label: Radically simplify, anchored on Jarvis
options.desc: 30 days: freeze new modules, records and rulings; archive what Jarvis does not reach; make the 35 declared gates run or delete them; rerun the 14/15 experiment blind; measure user-facing commit share weekly

options.label: The alternative as you wrote it
options.desc: Enforced gates + a CLI builder + an MCP builder with a fixed test suite; generate everything else

options.label: Continue as-is
options.desc: Keep building the framework in its current shape

options.label: Stop
options.desc: Freeze lev; build Jarvis features directly

items.title: How much of the naming work to do now
items.insight: Most N1 questions get smaller after a cut: fewer modules, fewer words to collide. The cheap mechanical pieces pay off either way.
items.detail:
- **Cheap and mechanical:** folder = noun, handler file = verb, a collision fails the build, operation ids carry the verb (done tonight for most commands).
- **Expensive:** moving entities out of dna/, moving task to workstream, the graph noun, state verbs on every entity.
- If you pick "simplify" above, the expensive items should wait until you know which modules survive.

options.label: Mechanical pieces now, park the rest
options.desc: Folder-noun convention + build-time collision error now; entity moves and state verbs after the cut

options.label: Do all of N1 now
options.desc: Rule every card below and build it

options.label: Park all of N1
options.desc: No naming work until the simplification is done

items.title: How do lev entities change state?
items.insight: When a task goes from in progress to done: its own command (`lev task done T1`) or one generic command (`lev task move T1 done`)? **Blind, 4 of 4 models expected named commands. Informed: 3 named (GLM, Opus, Fable) vs 1 generic move (codex).** The deciding point: agent clients approve tools by name, so named commands let you allow `block` and gate `archive`. Cost: about 30–40 more MCP tools across entity types. Note: Fable suggested keeping `workstream update --status` for one release as an alias, which breaks the no-shims hard-cutover rule; a ruling would drop that part.
items.detail:
- verified: informed picks. glm C (seat-state-verb-glm.md:1), opus-clean C (courier text), codex B (seat-state-verb-codex.md:1), fable-clean empty ('Complete.')
- verified: blind Part 2b, 4/4 C (seat-blind-cli-codex.md:31, seat-blind-cli-glm.md:29, plus both clean seats). 3 of 4 wanted `update --status` as a fallback
- verified: every command becomes one MCP tool (core/poly/src/surfaces/mcp/tools.ts:69-101) and one POST route (core/poly/src/surfaces/http/index.ts:158-172), so C needs no new plumbing and B needs no new plumbing either
- verified: today `lev task` has only `validate` (timeout 60 lev task --help); workstream uses a generic setter with active|paused|completed|superseded (core/workstream/src/schema.ts:26)
- verified: lifecycles declare states only (plugins/sdlc/config.yaml:73-79); task is an alias of execution_packet with no states (:80-89)
- verified: spec transitions are judged by a language-model prompt (plugins/sdlc/flows/spec-lifecycle.flow.yaml:70-106), which conflicts with the deterministic-gate doctrine (inference)
- **Why the pick:** C has 2 of 3 answering informed seats across two model families (Z.ai, Anthropic), and all 4 blind seats (three families) guessed it first. That matters for agents who will guess commands without reading docs. The deciding argument is that agent clients approve tools by name. Only C lets the operator auto-allow `task_block` while gating `task_archive`. The one dissenting seat (codex, B) names that same need as its own reason to switch to C. C also fits the existing one-command, one-tool, one-POST projection with no new plumbing, and it replaces the language-model transition judge with declared data. This is a majority, not consensus: the codex dissent is substantive (tool count, the need for revisions and idempotency on any option), and the second Anthropic seat is missing.
- **Confidence:** Medium. 2-1 among answering informed seats, with fable-clean missing; a B vote there would make the result divergent, 2-2. Blind 4/4 supports C. The main cost (tool count hurting agents) is unmeasured. Before this becomes law: re-run fable-clean, and adopt codex's revision and idempotency requirement whichever option wins.

options.label: A. Generic setter (`lev task update T1 --status done`)
options.desc: State is an editable field checked by a validator. One tool per type. No informed seat picked it. Opus-clean rejects it because Google's AIP-216 says state should be output only, and because 'status' already names the root command. 3 of 4 blind seats expected it only as a fallback.

options.label: B. Generic move (`lev task move T1 done`)
options.desc: Codex's pick. One `task_move` tool and one `POST /api/task/move` route per type, with mandatory declared from/to pairs, an expected revision and an idempotency key. The cost: no per-transition approval, a shared bag of arguments (`--on` only makes sense for blocked), and ambiguity when two events reach the same state (start and unblock both reach in_progress).

options.label: C. Named transitions (`lev task done T1`, `lev task block T1 --on T2`)
options.desc: The tribunal's leading pick (glm, opus-clean; 4/4 blind). Each lifecycle declares events as data. Each event becomes one CLI verb, MCP tool, SDK method and POST route. Illegal events fail with the current state and the allowed events. Costs about 30-40 MCP tools across types. Open sub-questions: task start vs work start, archive vs restore, reopen reason, renaming the status field to state.

options.label: D. Hybrid (C plus `lev task transition T1 <event>`)
options.desc: No seat picked it. Glm and opus-clean both reject it because one generic tool bypasses every per-tool approval. The blind seats' instinct to keep a generic fallback lands closest to this option.

options.label: E. Desired-state reconciliation (`lev task apply T1 --desired done`)
options.desc: No seat picked it. Codex defers it until durable reconciliation is actually needed. Glm and opus-clean reject it: it hides which events fired and their side effects while other agents act on the same entity, and it cannot collect per-event arguments.

items.title: What dna/ should be from now on
items.insight: dna/ mixes four things today: repo-wide intent, contracts for single modules, lists that running code reads, and 12k lines of outside notes. Running code reads 6 of its files and writes a seventh. The open-source copy ships only one of those six. In 5 of 8 facts checked, dna/ and module config disagree. Existing canon already says lists should be derived, and poly already builds commands from each module's config.yaml. So shrink dna/ to repo-wide intent that no running code imports. Each module then owns its own facts: entity types and states go in its config.yaml, CLI nouns come from its folder names (config.yaml only overrides), and its contract lives in a DNA file next to its code. Gates find all of this by folder convention, not from a list. Deleting dna/ outright leaves the thesis and vocabulary with no home. Generating config from dna/ brings back the registry you rejected.
items.detail:
- verified: dna/fractal.yaml:6 'Registries are derived artifacts'; dna/core/poly.dna.yaml:73-74 registry_is_derived
- verified: runtime reads at core/config/src/entity-roots.ts:112, core/config/src/config-loader.ts:1475, core/config/src/module-data-declarations.ts:279, core/lifecycle/src/vocab.ts:11, core/lifecycle/src/envelope.ts:15, core/uri/src/manifest.ts:61
- verified: runtime write at core/context-graph/src/handlers/ratchet-admission.ts:272 (dna/graph.yaml, via MCP tool at core/context-graph/src/surfaces/mcp.ts:220)
- verified: core/exec/src/execution/preflight.ts:66-80 puts the dna/gates.yaml criteria in front of every run prompt
- verified: tooling/oss-boundary.json:59-62 ships graph, entities, vernacular and testing only. Inference: core/lifecycle, core/uri and data declarations fail or fall back in a shipped install (not probed)
- verified (find/wc): 179 files, 39,714 lines. Repo-wide intent 16.7%, module contracts 30.6%, external notes 31.5% (class labels are judgment)
- **Why the pick:** This is the only option that meets all three of your constraints: dna is intent, dna is not imported, and there are no YAML registries. It reuses conventions that already work (poly reads config.yaml, sdlc declares entity_definitions, 3 plugins keep their own dna/, task packets use per-folder dna.yaml). It also fixes a real product bug: running code reads files the open-source copy does not ship.
- **Confidence:** medium-high. The direction is well supported. Still open: the name of the module-local DNA file, where the 14 skills intents go, and whether each of the 395 dna/core check commands is truly module-local (only 15 of 41 files mention no other module).

options.label: Intent root, modules own the rest
options.desc: dna/ keeps only repo-wide intent, about 40 files: thesis, graph principles, vernacular, the core and plugin contracts, cross-module architecture, testing taxonomy and authoring rules. Module contracts move next to their module; you pick the file name. Module facts go in config.yaml, and nouns come from folders. Runtime-read files move to their owners: emotes and the lifecycle schema to core/lifecycle, uri-schemes to core/uri, entities to workstream and sdlc. Data roots are derived from config data blocks. external/ leaves dna/. Order: cut the runtime reads first. Then move entities, with a scan-and-collide check in core/config. Then move module contracts and switch ratchet and validator discovery to a glob in the same commit. Delete entities.yaml last and replace its gate with a one-owner-per-type gate.

options.label: Colocate everything, dissolve dna/
options.desc: The same moves, and then thesis, vernacular and the architecture concepts also leave dna/, which is deleted. One rule covers everything. But repo-wide intent has no owning module, the authority stack in AGENTS.md, dna/index.yaml and lev-canon must be rewritten, and all 179 files move.

options.label: Central dna/, generated module config
options.desc: Keep dna/ as the place you write things and compile sections into config.yaml. Nothing moves, but it adds a codegen step and generated blocks inside hand-edited files, where hand edits get overwritten. It also brings back the authored registry you rejected.

options.label: Only cut runtime reads
options.desc: Move the 7 runtime-read files to their owners and leave dna/core and dna/plugins central. Cheap, and it fixes the shipped-install bug. But contracts stay in a different tree from their code, and the drift between lists and config continues.

items.title: Where entity types, states and roots should be declared
items.insight: Entity types are declared in at least five places: dna/entities.yaml, sdlc config.yaml, the project .lev/config.yaml, code type lists in plugins/now and core/flowmind, and 14 template folders. Plan states differ across four of these sources. Running code reads only one thing from dna/entities.yaml, the decision roots, and the code already has its own copy of them. The simplest home is the owning module's config.yaml. Each module declares the types it owns, with states, roots and a schema file in its own schemas/ folder. core/config builds the index by scanning module configs, as it already does for data blocks. If two modules claim one type, the build fails. The same check should cover CLI nouns, so the task entity and `lev task` cannot end up in different modules. Owners follow your 09-26 ruling: task and session to workstream, work to sdlc, vault to plugins/vault. Graph is still open.
items.detail:
- verified: dna/entities.yaml:31-286 (9 types, pm family, task block)
- verified: core/config/src/entity-roots.ts:53-62 and :112-125 read only the decision roots, and a hard-coded fallback copy already exists
- verified: plugins/sdlc/config.yaml:73-105 entity_definitions (precedent)
- verified: plan states disagree across plugins/sdlc/config.yaml:76, .lev/config.yaml:1101, dna/entities.yaml:90 and .lev/pm/plans/_template/schema.json
- verified: plugins/now/src/lev/entities.ts:10 still lists kinds that dna/entities.yaml:163-170 marks as consolidated
- verified: task storage path dna/entities.yaml:250 says .lev/tasks, but core/exec/src/exec-command/admission.ts:58 and disk use .lev/pm/tasks (285 dirs vs 1)
- **Why the pick:** It follows an existing precedent (sdlc entity_definitions) and reuses the core/config scanner. It puts states next to the code that enforces them, which is the likeliest fix for the four-way plan-state drift. And it matches the entity owners you already ruled.
- **Confidence:** medium-high. Open: the owner of graph and parity-entry, and whether project .lev/config.yaml may still override states or may only extend them.

options.label: Owning module's config.yaml declares its entities
options.desc: Each module's config.yaml gets an entities block, grown from sdlc's entity_definitions, with states, roots, naming and a schema path in the module's schemas/ folder. core/config builds the index by scanning, and two claims on one type fail the build (the same check covers CLI nouns). Entity identity addresses move to core/uri. The consolidated-types list moves to the vernacular retired list. A `--json` listing command replaces any YAML registry. The entities.yaml gate is replaced with a one-owner-per-type gate.

options.label: Folder-per-entity convention
options.desc: An entity type is a folder, <module>/entities/<type>/, holding its schema and template, with no list anywhere. This is the most file-based option, but it adds a new folder convention and more files. The existing .lev/pm/*/_template folders show the risk: type definitions mixed in with project data.

options.label: Code type lists in core/domain
options.desc: Entity kinds live in code only. This removes the YAML, but projects can no longer add types through config, and it breaks the rule that domain holds only types used by two or more contexts.

options.label: Keep dna/entities.yaml as a generated view
options.desc: Build it from module declarations for agents and the open-source copy. This keeps a registry-shaped file you said you do not want. A CLI listing does the same job without one.

items.title: How `lev <noun> <verb>` should come from the filesystem
items.insight: Today the root word is the handler file name, and whichever package is scanned first wins it. Losers vanish silently, which is why 19 words have several owners. Make the package folder the noun and the handler file the verb, and all 19 split onto separate paths with no config. Canon already asks for this, and HTTP, MCP and UI already work this way. The open piece is extra nouns: workstream will own task and session, and autoresearch presents experiment and content. Recommended: a handler subfolder with no index file is an extra noun. A subfolder with an index file stays one multi-file verb, as today. A one-line config override only renames a module's own noun (graph, maybe evolve or hand). Every choice here needs your open fork ruled yes: may a module claim a noun other than its folder name? The worker command `lev graph patch` is not covered; the graph card decides it.
items.detail:
- verified: core/poly/src/registry/commands.ts:190 makes the root word the handler file name; :200 and :231 let the first writer win
- verified (this merge): commands.ts:176-184 already treats a handler folder with index.js/index.ts as one command. core/index/src/handlers/find/ is 8 files under index.js; plugins/sdlc/src/handlers/session/ has index.ts plus bootstrap.ts
- verified: commands.ts:369, :387, :398 and :401 already scope HTTP, MCP and UI by package
- verified: dna/core/poly.dna.yaml:266 'lev workstream create/show/list/update by fractal convention' (aspirational); dna/fractal.yaml:129-139 says the module name is the address segment, with no stutter
- verified (simulation against the real loader): 19 of 19 contested words resolve, and 5 same-package duplicates appear. 1 is real: plugins/browser browse.ts vs browser.ts
- verified: 0 of 108 config.yaml files declare a noun today
- **Why the pick:** This is pure file-based routing, which is what you asked for. It keeps `lev task validate` stable for the 22 files that cite it, handles multi-noun packages like autoresearch without a list, and needs at most a handful of one-line renames. Collisions fail at build time instead of being settled by load order.
- **Confidence:** medium. The counts come from a simulation against the real loader's claims. The 'same stem' test is a heuristic (it decides validator/validate and browse/browser), the key name is not in the vernacular yet, and the noun-claim fork is unruled.

options.label: Folder is the noun, plus a one-line rename
options.desc: Noun = package folder, verb = handler file. A repeat or same-stem word collapses (the stutter rule), and any collision fails the build. The config.yaml line `poly: noun: graph` renames a module's own noun (the key name is yours to pick). Resolves 19 of 19 conflicts. But task and session are reachable only as `lev workstream task validate`, which breaks the 22 files citing `lev task validate`, and autoresearch cannot express three nouns.

options.label: Above, plus index-less handler subfolders as extra nouns
options.desc: The same as the first option, plus `src/handlers/<noun>/<verb>.ts` with no index file gives a package another noun with zero config. core/workstream/src/handlers/task/validate.ts serves `lev task validate`, and autoresearch uses content/ and experiment/ subfolders. A folder that has an index file stays one multi-file verb, so core/index's find/ needs no flattening. Two packages claiming the same noun fails the build. sdlc's session/ moves to workstream per the ruling.

options.label: Per-package noun list in config.yaml
options.desc: `poly: nouns: [workstream, task, session]`. This is config, not convention. Each handler still needs a mapping to its noun, which brings back a small registry in every package.

options.label: Keep flat roots, fix conflicts by renaming
options.desc: The 19 conflicts and the load-order winners stay until someone renames them. This contradicts the ruled `lev <noun> <verb>` grammar and the rule that a collision fails the build.

items.title: Getting `lev task` out of orchestration
items.insight: `lev task` runs core/orchestration's task handler today (a live probe reports it as orchestration.task). You ruled that task belongs to workstream, not orchestration. But canon gives the readiness logic behind the command (950 lines) to orchestration, and workstream is not allowed to import orchestration. The smallest honest move is to relocate only the thin CLI handler and file a fork to allow that one import edge. Moving the logic too means rewriting ownership canon and touching about 23 files plus 20 test fixtures. This keeps `lev task validate` working only if you pick the subfolder option on the noun card. The wider orchestration cleanup is a separate job: about 47% of its code looks misplaced, including git worktrees, a persistent queue, a session writer and the CDO runner.

items.title: What 'belong to poly' means
items.insight: 'Belong to poly' means no single module owns the word; the host does. core/poly is the program that reads every module's config.yaml and handler files and builds the lev CLI, MCP tools and HTTP routes from them. The host answers a verb in one of two ways. It can answer by itself: help lists what poly built, and version reads lev's own version. Or it can fan out: ask every module the same question and merge the replies. Today only help and version are poly's. `lev status` belongs to core/daemon only because core packages sort first, and it fails with exit 2. `lev doctor` is core/build's fixed checklist. Your ruling makes status and doctor fan-outs: each module ships a small probe, and poly collects the results. Seven modules claim the bare word status today, and 18 declare some kind of status command.

- verified: core/daemon/config.yaml:58-60 plus commands.ts:231 first-writer-wins. Live `lev status --json` returned UNIMPLEMENTED_COMMAND_SURFACE, exit 2
- verified: core/build/src/handlers/doctor.ts:585-607 hardcodes 6 categories. Live run gave 35 checks: 12 pass, 23 warn
- verified: 7 modules claim the bare word status (daemon, orchestration, autowiki, genui-exec-daemon, platforms, watchdog, workflow-orchestrator). 18 modules declare some status handler, sdk entry or surface, for example plugins/vault/config.yaml:80

items.title: lev init / lev upgrade, and lev sdlc work vs lev work
items.insight: Your ruling allows three kinds of root word: a module's own name (lev exec), poly's own verbs (help, version), and fan-outs (status, doctor). lev init and lev upgrade are none of these. Both belong to core/build, so the strict rule makes them lev build init and lev build upgrade. Today lev upgrade quietly runs install, so the real upgrade handler never runs. core/onboarding also holds install and init logic, but nothing calls it. Cleanest fix: installing and upgrading lev is the host's own job, like version, so add two host verbs. That changes your ruled list of four, so record it as a new ruling. Work is simpler. You gave work to sdlc and preferred lev sdlc work, which is plain noun plus verb under the folder rule. Root lev work and the go alias go away. Today lev sdlc work fails.

items.title: Who answers search, find and research
items.insight: Single owner means one module answers. lev research asks only plugins/research. Fan-out means one command asks many modules and merges what comes back. Local search already fans out, but inside one module: lev find is core/index, which queries its own sources (code, docs, tasks, memory, graph) and merges the results. A live run just hit 3 of them. A root fan-out would duplicate that work. Meanwhile 'search' means three different things. CLI lev search goes to a platform-API catalog and fails. The help text calls it index search. The MCP tool lev_search runs index find. 'Context' has no search owner either: plugins/context compresses conversations, and root lev context is code-graph symbol lookup. Simplest answer: no root search. Use lev research for the web and lev index find for local search.

items.title: core/security: what it is, and where taint + SSRF should live
items.insight: core/security is a spike from March, merged on 09-26, that bundles seven small defensive helpers. Nothing imports it and it is not in the pnpm workspace, so CI never builds or tests it. Two pieces are new. Taint labels mark data as trusted or untrusted and carry the mark onto anything made from it. The SSRF check refuses URLs that point at private networks or cloud metadata. Both have passing tests (25 of 25 under bun). The other five either duplicate an owner that already exists or have no tests and no users. The injection scanner copies guardrails, Receipt copies EffectReceipt and EvalDecision, and the hash chain copies the Rust lev-audit crate. Security already lives in three plugins: guardrails filters LLM input and output, defendr scans code before install, and vault holds secrets. A new plugins/security would be a fourth home.

items.title: Who owns the noun "graph"
items.insight: 'Graph' means at least twelve things here. The canonical one is the knowledge graph in core/context-graph, and the boundary file names that package as its owner. But today `lev graph` is served by core/exec and does one thing: a worker submits its proof claim, and every worker is told to type `lev graph patch`. context-graph has its own, different graph-patch command that applies raw graph edits. It sits at `lev graph-patch` next to 15 other graph-* words that nothing references. If context-graph simply takes the noun graph, `lev graph patch` would silently switch to that raw-edit command and break every worker. Separately, code-graph hides discourse-graph's query and analyze commands. So context-graph can own graph only with one recorded exception, or the worker command has to be renamed.
items.detail:
- verified: core/exec/config.yaml:125-167 binds `graph` to src/handlers/done.ts as lev.graph.patch (http /api/lev/graph/patch, mcp lev_graph_patch). Live `lev graph --help` confirms
- verified (this merge): core/exec/src/handlers/done.ts:20 and :156 submit the Claim through exec's claim-admission, which writes the ledger
- verified (this merge): core/context-graph/src/handlers/graph-patch.ts:451-463 is a separate exported handler. It applies raw JSON graph operations, returns the schema when given no operations, and rejects claim-scoped use. So it is not the worker claim path
- verified: dna/architecture/core-boundaries/concept.yaml:128-130 and :242-244 give context-graph entity_graph, graph_queries and knowledge_graph
- verified: dna/vernacular.yaml:167-168 defines graph_patch as 'an aligned proposal expressed as graph operations'
- verified: worker contract at core/orchestration/src/completion/completion-instruction.ts:97,102 and core/domain/src/claim.ts:75. The research counted 10 non-test files citing `lev graph patch`; this merge's rg over core, plugins and .lev/flows found 13
- **Why the pick:** graph + patch is the right noun and verb (a claim is a proposed graph change), and context-graph is the canon owner. Keeping `lev graph patch` byte-identical avoids touching the worker contract, which every dispatched worker depends on. The price is one recorded binding exception, forced by the rule that only exec writes the ledger, plus renaming context-graph's raw patch command. The strict option is purer but spends a worker-contract rename to avoid that exception.
- **Confidence:** medium-low. The facts and import limits are verified. Unverified: whether poly can bind one verb under a noun to a different module, and whether context-graph's raw graph-patch command has MCP or script users that a rename would break.

options.label: context-graph owns `lev graph`; exec keeps `patch` as one recorded exception
options.desc: The 17 graph-* roots become `lev graph <verb>` (query, export, health and so on), which is free because nothing references them. First rename or hide context-graph's own raw graph-patch command (the new name is yours). `lev graph patch` stays byte-identical for workers and is still served by core/exec, because only exec writes the ledger. code-graph and discourse-graph go to their own folder-name roots, which ends the shadowing. Needs the noun-claim fork ruled yes, plus one recorded exception to 'one module per noun'.
